Experiments on KernelBench show that our approach improves kernel optimization over fixed profiling configurations under constrained profiling budgets. These results suggest that hardware profiling should evolve from static metric collection toward profiling reasoning, making profiling itself a new dimension for improving kernel optimization. The codes are available at https://github.com/Satissss/AutoProfiler.

Health system innovations aimed at improving healthcare access are complex with potential for unintended consequences. There is a need for real-time evaluation which captures evolving contexts and impacts. This study presents experiences—both successes and failures—at extending the sensemaking methodology from our previous work into a large scale health ecosystem for monitoring, evaluation and learning in such contexts. Between May 2022 and October 2023, we explored the feasibility of using a sensemaking methodological approach to provide near real-time feedback on a large-scale health system innovation. We designed two complexity-informed data collection instruments using the Cognitive Edge SenseMaker® tool, and attempted to: 1) operationalize them across diverse patient populations and providers; and 2) engage with stakeholders in collaborative sensemaking of the insights from the data. Between May 2022 and October 2023, test data yielded 221 patient and 104 provider entries regarding surgical referral experiences. Attempts to scale the data collection instruments within formal healthcare channels to reach a diverse representation of patients and providers were unsuccessful. We pivoted to capture information on the impacts of our enacted data collection strategies. From these efforts, we generated a diagrammatic representation of the sensemaking methodological approach, namely the Illuminate 360°. This approach consists of an iterative cycle: data collection, analysis, monitoring/reflection, decision-making, and action planning. Central to this is the integration of regular sensemaking sessions with relevant parties, which facilitates clarity on the phenomenon of interest and insights for action. While scaling up the methodology through formal channels proved unfeasible within the project’s parameters, our findings offer critical insights into building situational awareness for complex healthcare interventions. We demonstrate that the Illuminate 360° approach, when grounded in implementation science frameworks and theories, can generate the timely, co-created data necessary to inform healthcare improvement and support data-driven decision-making.

Digital-based Islamic Religious Education (IRE) provides opportunities to use learning activity data to understand student engagement and learning outcomes. However, high levels of digital activity do not necessarily indicate deep cognitive engagement or successful learning. This study aims to analyze the use of learning analytics to examine student engagement and learning outcomes in digital-based IRE. It employs a qualitative approach using the library research method. Data were obtained by reviewing relevant literature on learning analytics, student engagement, learning outcomes, and digital-based IRE, and were analyzed descriptively through the identification and synthesis of findings. The results indicate that learning analytics can be used to identify behavioral engagement through access to learning materials, task completion, and participation in assessments, as well as to examine cognitive engagement through students’ understanding of learning materials and the quality of their responses. The use of these data can help educators identify learning difficulties, provide feedback, and determine appropriate instructional follow-up. Nevertheless, the relationship between engagement and learning outcomes must be interpreted cautiously because it is influenced by various factors. Digital activity data are also insufficient to assess all aspects of religious understanding and character development. This study concludes that learning analytics has the potential to support pedagogical decision-making in digital-based IRE, provided that data quality, privacy, and the learning context are taken into account.

Construction safety management still struggles to produce daily safety bulletins (DSBs), structured daily communications that identify site-specific hazards, convey safety protocols, and set preventive measures for workers. Manual DSB creation takes 2-3 hours daily and yields inconsistent quality, with 25% of crews never conducting pretask planning (Olson et al., 2016), diverting safety personnel from field supervision. This study proposes the Lightweight Multi-Agent DSB System (LM-DSB), which integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a locally deployable Large Language Model (LLM) to automate DSB generation on consumer-grade personal computers. LM-DSB coordinates specialized planner, researcher, and writer agents in a hierarchical architecture, enhanced by domain-specific fine-tuning on construction safety documentation and RAG grounding in 37 health, safety, and environment (HSE) documents. A two-phase validation assessed feasibility. Phase 1 comparative evaluation showed the multi-agent RAG system (Llama 3-8B) outperformed all alternative configurations, with strong lexical alignment and coherence (TF-IDF: 0.70, BLEU: 0.39, ROUGE-1: 0.66) and near-complete document generation (length ratio: 1.01 vs. 0.39 for single-agent RAG). Phase 2 expert evaluation (N=40) confirmed practical acceptability (mean scores 3.50-4.20 on a 5-point scale), particularly in regulatory compliance (4.20) and factual accuracy (4.10). The findings show that architectural design enables lightweight models to handle safety-critical documentation on consumer-grade hardware, advancing technology democratization in construction safety management. Limitations include knowledge base scope, language constraints, and lack of field deployment validation; future work should address multimodal integration and workflow adoption.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Quantum technologies (QT) are increasingly being taken up in artistic practices, for example in the form of visual artworks or quantum computer music. However, more comprehensive empirical studies on the temporal development and the different forms of QT-related art are still lacking. Therefore, this study conducted a systematic mapping and classification of QT-related artworks. To this end, a medium-independent corpus was established, and the artworks were classified into four categories: QT-Inspired, QT-Sourced, Simulated QT, and QT-Generated. This classification was LLM-assisted and checked against human-coded reference data as well as through manual review of unclear cases. In total, 281 QT-related artworks from 2010 to August 2025 were identified. The corpus shows a substantial increase in QT-related artworks since 2019, with a considerable share attributed to only a few artists. The different forms of QT relations coexist, while an increasing use of active hardware-based and simulated processes in artistic practices can be documented, particularly since 2021. Although no clear development trajectories between these categories can be identified, the observed development coincides with advances in QT and their improved accessibility. Thus, this study provides an empirical basis for further analyzing the development of QT-related art, the possible emergence of a "quantum art scene," and the reciprocal relationships between art and quantum technologies.

Maritime Information Management (MIM) has emerged as one of the most transformative domains in contemporary maritime operations. As global supply chains become increasingly interconnected, port networks more tightly coupled, and vessel traffic more congested, the maritime sector has moved decisively from a hardware-centric industry to a data-driven ecosystem. At its core, MIM concerns the systematic collection, processing, dissemination, and governance of maritime information to enhance operational efficiency, situational awareness, safety, resilience, and decision-making across ocean-based and coastal systems. It integrates technologies, organisational practices, decision-support tools, and behavioural processes that allow maritime stakeholders – ports, shipping companies, pilots, regulators, and emergency managers – to operate with higher levels of synchronisation and foresight ( Heilig & Voß, 2017 ).

Third-party community-based bots are central to how social platforms such as Discord work. They moderate content, manage roles, play music, and support AI-assisted conversations across millions of servers. Yet when a bot is installed in a server, it can access messages, user profiles, and server metadata concerning members who did not participate in the installation decision, with no standardized way to communicate the associated security and privacy implications. In this paper, we analyze 23,102 third-party Discord bots and 183,142 user reviews spanning 49 detected languages and five years of feedback (2021-2026). We employ LLM-based knowledge distillation and fine-tune a DeBERTa-based classifier to identify candidate security and privacy (S&P)-relevant reviews. After manually validating the complete classifier-positive set, we retain 8,832 reviews identified as S&P-relevant, representing an observed pipeline yield of 4.82%, and map them to a 31-theme S&P taxonomy extending prior work. Our results show that S&P-related reviews focus heavily on Data Sharing (30.5%) and Data Collection (16.2%). Confession and anonymity bots have pipeline-identified SPRRs above 50%, more than ten times the ecosystem-wide pipeline yield of 4.82%. Star ratings may obscure the frequency and valence of S&P-related discussion, while conventional metadata features, such as permission count and administrator status, show only weak associations with user-reported S&P concerns. We then build BotLens, a proof-of-concept auditing framework that combines review-derived S&P signals with bot metadata to provide on-demand decision support for the community-based bot ecosystem. BotLens exposes six tools through a Model Context Protocol server, supporting bot-level checkups, server-wide comparison, and integration with AI agents.

As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Mining workers face high psychosocial risks, yet stigma and limited mental health literacy keep many of them from seeking help. This community service program set out to improve mental health literacy, self-recognition of stress, and access to psychological services among employees of PT X. It combined four components: a psychoeducational seminar on mental health at the workplace, a stress assessment using the DASS-42 stress subscale, individual psychological counseling, and a pocket guide, the Wellness Support Guide. The program was evaluated descriptively and qualitatively, and all components were delivered as planned. Employees gained a basic understanding of mental health and occupational stress, a self-administered early detection tool, and a clear route to counseling. The assessment worked as an entry point to counseling for employees who needed it, while the guide kept the psychoeducational message within reach after the seminar. The program recommends periodic screening, supervisor training, peer supporters trained in Psychological First Aid, integration of psychosocial risks into occupational health and safety management, and a pre-post design in future evaluations.

Every neural-network training run produces not only a model, but also evidence about how models learn. Can these accumulated experiments enable us to predict and compare new training runs before executing them? We study meta-models: models that predict the learning behavior of other models. From this perspective, final-performance prediction, learning-curve prediction, and hyperparameter selection are different queries to the same training response function. We take a first, humble empirical step toward this goal: treating real language-model training records as native numeric data, we find that an off-the-shelf tabular in-context learner, TabPFN, can match or outperform a fine-tuned LLM meta-model in multiple evaluated settings. Whereas recent work fine-tunes LLMs on tokenized configurations at a cost of tens to hundreds of GPU-hours, TabPFN requires seconds of fit-and-predict time without task-specific weight updates. We argue that meta-modeling is better treated as its own numeric modality rather than as a text task for LLMs. Going one step further, augmenting TabPFN with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) further improves accuracy on selected prediction tasks. Finally, we pre-registered a forecast of the Marin Hero Run, a 535B-parameter public training run, whose ground truth is revealed point by point as training progresses, putting meta-model predictions to the test against training outcomes not yet observed at the time of forecasting.

This study evaluated energy expenditure while walking with a powered ankle exoskeleton in middle-aged adults. Participants wore a bilateral ankle exoskeleton. Metabolic cost was measured via indirect calorimetry. Participants walked on a treadmill without the exoskeleton and with the exoskeleton unpowered, powered, and unpowered again. Net metabolic cost of transport (MCOT) was calculated. Behaviors exhibited include a decrease in MCOT, an increase in MCOT, and initial changes that diminished with time. This variability may be explained by differences in adaptation times, which may be more pronounced among middle-aged adults due to age-related changes in gait and declines in neuromuscular and sensory function. These results underscore the importance of age-related considerations in training protocols, recognizing that middle-aged adults may require longer, more structured training than young adults. Insufficient adaptation may prevent users from experiencing metabolic improvements that could contribute to reduced injury risk and lower rates of musculoskeletal disorders.

The growing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into human cognitive activities, including problem-solving, decision-making, learning and information processing, has raised important questions about cognitive work allocation, metacognitive control and independent performance. Although GenAI can enhance efficiency by reducing cognitive demands, excessive reliance may weaken users’ engagement in reasoning, verification and independent task execution. This review examines the relationship between GenAI use and human cognition, with particular emphasis on cognitive offloading, appropriate reliance, over-reliance, automation bias and independent performance. Drawing on existing research, it explores how the effects of cognitive offloading depend on task characteristics and the distribution of cognitive responsibility between users and AI systems. The review further considers interventions such as think-first strategies, cognitive forcing functions, reflection, verification prompts and adaptive scaffolding that aim to preserve human cognitive engagement while benefiting from AI assistance. In addition, it examines behavioural telemetry including prompt intent, interaction timing, response editing and verification activities as a potential means of identifying patterns of engagement and reliance during multi-turn human AI interactions. These observable behaviours are treated as indirect indicators rather than definitive measures of internal cognitive processes. The review highlights the importance of evaluating not only task performance with AI assistance but also users’ ability to perform independently when such assistance is unavailable. It identifies a need for integrated frameworks that connect cognitive work allocation, metacognition, observable interaction patterns, reliance calibration and independent performance over time. Such frameworks may support the development of human-centred GenAI systems that improve task effectiveness while maintaining users’ critical thinking, self-regulation and cognitive autonomy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) tutors remove exactly the effort that learning requires: students adopt the instant answer, offload the reasoning to the model, and retain less. Friction-based tutors reverse the offloading, yet learners disengage from unbounded friction. This paper tests whether game-structural mechanics—checkpoints, low-stakes failure with retry, and a rescue that guarantees completion—hold the learner inside a tutor's deliberate friction. In a multi-agent simulation of 180 students (three independent draws of 60) across six levels of seeded misconception burden, each student works the same ten-part physics problem under three tutor conditions: instant answer, strict Socratic, and a ten-checkpoint quest in which every part is unlocked only by the student's own attempt. The quest condition removes the measured offloading: students produce 0.999 of the solution steps against 0.302 under the instant answer, self-reported offloading is 1.48 versus 5.58 on a 6-point scale, and every student names the instant-answer condition as the one in which they offloaded most. Structuring the friction also removes its cost: quest sessions complete in 100 percent of cases, against a 14.4 percent abandonment rate in the strict condition, where sessions that run long end when the student's reported motivation reaches the floor. Both friction conditions raise the unaided posttest far above the shared pretest (0.928 and 0.885 versus 0.455); the instant-answer condition reaches only 0.563. Friction that is structured as bounded progression holds the learner inside productive struggle without the attrition that plain withholding carries.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examined how students’ motivational regulation during creative writing was organized when generative artificial intelligence (AI) was unavailable or optionally available. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), motivation was conceptualized as configurations of intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, introjected regulation, and external regulation. The sample comprised 406 students in Grades 5–8 who completed comparable creative writing tasks without AI (Time 1) and with optional AI access (Time 2). Using a micro-longitudinal, person-centered design, latent profile analyses identified motivational configurations and examined psychological need satisfaction and academic achievement as predictors of profile membership; degree of AI use was examined at Time 2. Mean levels of motivational regulation remained largely stable, whereas person-centered analyses revealed heterogeneity in regulatory configurations and differences in the prevalence of comparable profiles. Autonomy satisfaction declined at Time 2, while higher need satisfaction, particularly autonomy and competence, was associated with more self-determined configurations. End-of-term grades differentiated profile membership at both occasions. Degree of AI use did not significantly predict profile membership. Cross-context analyses showed correspondence alongside redistribution. Because full profile similarity was unsupported, these patterns were interpreted descriptively rather than as transitions between equivalent latent states. AI availability coincided with configurational differences not apparent from mean-level analyses. The findings distinguish AI availability from usage intensity and suggest that AI-supported writing should be understood in relation to psychological needs, academic functioning, and regulatory demands surrounding support, delegation, authorship, and agency.

Social value creation is a stated priority in commercial property and ESG agendas, yet little is known about why owners and occupiers pursue social initiatives or what sustains them. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT) and its sub-theory of organismic integration, this study examines the motivations underpinning social value in Auckland's prime office market, New Zealand. Eleven semi-structured interviews with eighteen owners, occupiers and agents across ten organisations were analysed thematically alongside corporate sustainability reporting. Motivations cluster around four drivers: market obligations, environmental imperatives, employee priorities and socio-cultural responsibilities. These range from external and introjected regulation through identified and integrated forms to, rarely, intrinsic motivation. Owners span the full range, whereas occupiers stabilise at identified regulation centred on employee well-being and organisational culture. This difference is positional rather than dispositional, since participants holding both roles express different motivations depending on the role from which they speak. Motivation also varies spatially: provision closest to the leasing transaction is the most externally regulated and provision furthest from it the most integrated. The study extends motivational theory to the commercial built environment, proposes a dual-stakeholder framework, and shows why assessments based on whether provision exists cannot distinguish durable from compliance-driven social value.

Abstract Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a strong popularity bias in recommendation tasks, often over-recommending mainstream items while under-representing user-aligned but less popular content. To address this limitation, we propose a multi-stage alignment pipeline for debiasing LLM-based movie recommenders, consisting of preference extraction from user histories, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for behavioral grounding, and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) for bias-corrective alignment toward less-popular yet topically relevant items. By explicitly separating grounding from bias correction, the framework enables stable and controllable improvements in exposure fairness. In addition to intrinsic alignment, we systematically compare our approach against classical post-hoc debiasing methods, including popularity-aware re-ranking, to examine trade-offs between recommendation quality and exposure balance. Experiments on MovieLens, Netflix, and Flickscore demonstrate that multi-stage alignment achieves substantial gains in novelty and catalog coverage while maintaining competitive accuracy and offering advantages over simpler exposure-adjustment baselines. These results position multi-stage LLM alignment as a principled and scalable strategy for mitigating popularity bias in generative recommender systems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/krishnakantx/debiased-llm-recsys.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The World Health Organization (WHO) created the Surgical Safety Checklist (SSC) to make patients safer, help teams talk to each other, and cut down on issues that may be avoided during surgery. The SSC comprises three critical phases “sign in” (before anesthesia), “time out” (before incision), and “sign out” (before the patient leaves the operating room) each designed to ensure adherence to essential safety steps. Even though there is proof across the world that the checklist works, people in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), including Nigeria, have not always followed it. Reported checklist use in LMICs is consistently and substantially lower than in high-income settings [1]. This study examined the obstacles to adherence and completeness of the Surgical Safety Checklist (SSC) among surgical team members in two tertiary institutions in Nigeria. A qualitative exploratory design was utilized for this study. Key informant interviews were performed with 13 participants, comprising consultants, resident physicians, nurses, and anesthetists from Obafemi Awolowo University Teaching Hospitals Complex (OAUTHC), Ile-Ife, Osun State and Ekiti State University Teaching Hospital (EKSUTH), Ekiti, Ekiti State. Data were gathered by a semi-structured interview guide, transcribed verbatim, and subjected to thematic analysis. Data collection continued until thematic saturation was achieved, defined as the point at which no new themes or insights emerged from subsequent interviews. Three main themes emerged: (1) systemic and workflow constraints, such as not enough staff, too much work, time pressure, and emergencies; (2) human factors and team dynamics, such as poor cooperation, weak accountability, and hierarchical barriers; and (3) training, awareness, and attitudes, such as not enough training, checklist fatigue, and the idea that the SSC is just a box to check. These findings indicate varying levels of preparedness for SSC implementation across the two institutions, particularly in terms of staffing, training, and workflow integration. These obstacles hindered the continuous and comprehensive utilization of the SSC in both institutions, with a more significant impact observed at EKSUTH. Both hospitals have adopted the SSC, but systemic, behavioral, and organizational hurdles make it hard to apply it to its full potential. To improve the culture of safety in Nigerian tertiary hospitals, leaders need to be committed, personnel need to be trained, workflow support must be improved, and positive safety norms need to be reinforced. Adapting the SSC to local workflows rather than relying solely on the generic WHO format may further improve adherence and sustainability.

The management of occupational health and safety measurement equipment in educational institutions often faces challenges related to borrowing and returning records, calibration tracking, and access to equipment information, resulting in inefficient management. This research and development study aimed to develop an integrated web-based occupational health and safety measurement equipment management system combining QR Code-based equipment identification, equipment lifecycle management, and LINE Messaging API communication, and to evaluate system quality, user satisfaction, and factors associated user acceptance. The participants consisted of three groups: three personnel involved in equipment management, three information technology experts, and thirty system users. The research instruments included a semi-structured interview form, a system quality evaluation form, and a user satisfaction questionnaire. Data were analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson's correlation coefficient, and multiple linear regression analysis. The developed system consisted of eight main modules covering user management, equipment information management, borrowing and returning, calibration, maintenance, QR code management, LINE notification, and administrative reporting. The overall system quality evaluated by experts was at the highest level (mean = 4.88, SD = 0.20), and overall user satisfaction was also at the highest level (mean = 4.85, SD = 0.33). System usability showed a strong positive correlation with user acceptance (r = 0.81, p < 0.01). Moreover, system usability, interface design, and system reliability and security jointly explained 72.0% of the variance in user acceptance. These findings indicate that the developed system achieved high levels of perceived quality and user acceptance, while providing an integrated digital approach to equipment identification, lifecycle management, user communication, and learning support for occupational health and safety measurement equipment in higher education.

**Background:** Vaccination is a key element of occupational health programmes, especially for workers exposed to infectious hazards and those caring for people at high risk of severe vaccine-preventable disease. Uptake depends on access, organizational and behavioral factors, confidence, and legal and ethical context. **Objective:** To synthesize evidence on occupational immunization strategies for healthcare workers and other groups with relevant biological exposure, integrating clinical, organizational, behavioral, ethical, and legal considerations. **Methods:** A structured narrative review examined literature and official guidance on occupational and adult vaccination, workplace interventions, vaccine hesitancy, biological risk, informed consent, and vaccination policy. Evidence from January 2020 to February 2025 was prioritized, supplemented by key earlier studies and authoritative legal and policy documents. Heterogeneous findings were synthesized thematically. **Results:** Systematic reviews and meta-analyses suggest that multicomponent interventions can improve healthcare-worker vaccination uptake, although effects vary by setting, vaccine, baseline coverage, and implementation. Convenient access, reminders, active invitation, and behavioral facilitation are most useful when paired with credible communication and institutional support. Ethical and legal sources stress proportionality, informed consent, confidentiality, equity, and context-specific assessment of restrictive policies. Spanish occupational-health law centers prevention on risk assessment and worker protection while safeguarding health surveillance and confidentiality. **Conclusions:** Occupational vaccination should form part of biological-risk management rather than operate solely as an annual campaign. The most transferable model combines risk assessment, equitable access, behavioral support, evidence-based counseling, confidentiality, and continuous evaluation. Restrictive measures require separate legal and ethical assessment and should not be generalized across jurisdictions or occupational settings.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Creating is one of the three core competencies of educational technology, alongside using and managing, yet many educators still find it difficult to produce digital learning resources that are engaging, aesthetic, and grounded in visual message design principles. This study aims to describe the conceptual foundation of Creating competence, analyze the use of Canva as a digital learning resource, and present a practical guide for producing it. A descriptive qualitative approach was applied through a literature review and documentation of a case study on Creating an educational infographic with Canva, guided by the ADDIE model. Data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The findings show that Canva meets four selection criteria for learning resources, namely alignment with learning objectives, readability and ergonomics, multi-platform flexibility, and visual message design, and that it supports the principles of behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, and Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning. The case study produced a three-part infographic on the Creating, using, and managing domains, and showed that artificial intelligence can assist the production of visual assets provided its outputs are verified. The study covers the analysis, design, and development stages only; implementation and evaluation with learners are recommended for further research.

To speed up the mobility transition, organisations can play a key role. Three intervention studies involving electric vehicles and shared bikes show which factors enable or hinder change from the perspective of employees and executives.A rapid and societally supported mobility transition in Germany requires more than technological innovation or individual behaviour change. Organisations can play a central role, as they shape employees' everyday mobility through infrastructures, incentives, and corporate sustainability strategies. This paper investigates the role of organisations in a mixed-methods study of interventions with e-cars, e-scooters, and bike sharing in three urban business parks. Data were analysed at the micro (individual), meso (organisation), and macro (sociotechnical landscape) levels. From an organisational perspective, key enabling factors include top-down management support for employee-based sustainability initiatives, the integration of mobility measures into wider sustainability strategies, psychologically safe environments for testing new technologies, and favourable macro-level framework conditions, such as equitable incentive structures and fewer bureaucratic hurdles. Key hindering factors include costs and concerns about greenwashing.

The presented work is devoted to the study of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostics physicians in the context of organizational and ergonomic working conditions. The object of the research is emotional exhaustion as a basic component of professional burnout syndrome. The author examines in detail the specificity of the work of this professional group, which includes working in darkened rooms, forced static posture, high patient flow, and lack of micropauses. Special attention is paid to the fact that these factors have not yet been the subject of separate quantitative analysis. The paper analyzes the relationship between working conditions and the severity of emotional exhaustion, and substantiates the need to revise existing workload standards. The key emphasis is placed on the fact that emotional exhaustion in this category of specialists has not only a psychological, but also a pronounced organizational and environmental nature. A total of 228 functional diagnostics physicians were examined. The MBI questionnaire adapted by N.E. Vodopyanova, an author-developed questionnaire of somatic and sensory symptoms, and a brief questionnaire of organizational characteristics were used. Dispersion, correlation, and multiple regression analyses were applied. The scientific novelty of this study lies in the fact that it is the first to quantitatively assess the contribution of organizational factors to the development of emotional exhaustion in functional diagnostic physicians, as well as to compare objective workload parameters with the severity of sensory-muscular complaints. The relationship between the number of studies and the level of exhaustion is shown to be linear. The authors' key findings are as follows: with a workload of over 20 studies per day, the average exhaustion score reaches 32.1 ± 8.9, compared to 21.4 ± 8.7 with a workload of up to 10 studies. Continuous work without a microbreak for more than 60 minutes was found to increase exhaustion by 6.8 points. The strongest predictors were weekly workload (β = 0.31) and the duration of uninterrupted visual work (β = 0.27). Based on the data obtained, recommendations for optimizing the work regime were substantiated: no more than 15 examinations per shift, a mandatory five-minute break after each hour of work, and limiting continuous visual load to 45–50 minutes. These recommendations can be taken into account when developing local regulations for medical organizations.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article is a hypothesis-generating perspective rather than a controlled study, and its claims should be read as propositions for testing. Large language models produce text with a recognizable linguistic signature that differs from much human academic prose in word choice, sentence shape, and discourse rhythm. We asked whether passive reading of artificial intelligence (AI)-associated text can change how people write, even when they never use a chatbot themselves. We defined passive exposure as reading text that carries AI-associated features without using an AI tool on one’s own writing, and we separated it from AI-assisted editing and hybrid human-AI authorship. The question grew from unsystematic expert observations made in teaching and editorial work, which motivate the hypothesis but do not test it. Large-scale corpus analyses show a sharp post-2022 rise in AI-associated vocabulary in published abstracts and in conference peer reviews. We organized the argument as one pathway running from exposure through internalization to convergence. The paper described candidate linguistic markers of AI text and explained how statistical and implicit learning, mere exposure and frequency effects, linguistic alignment, and experience-dependent neuroplasticity could carry the effect, although their application to AI text remains untested. We then considered what convergence would mean for assessment, stylistic diversity, and cognitive engagement, and we weighed alternative explanations, competing human input, and the confound with direct AI use. We closed with ten testable predictions, their practical limits, and propositions for writing education, so that the question can be studied while pre-AI baselines remain measurable.

Abstract Third-party dependency vulnerabilities are de- tected reliably but repaired badly. Scanners identify the ad- visory and point at a fixed version range; they rarely establish whether the upgrade is safe for the project that consumes it, and almost never repair the source code that the upgrade breaks. Recent work responds by delegating the decision to large language model (LLM) agents, yet a large-scale study of agent-authored pull requests finds that agents select already- vulnerable versions more often than humans do, and that remediating those selections disproportionately requires major- version upgrades. A benchmark of 203 real dependency-upgrade tasks reports that the strongest coding-agent configuration completes barely half of them, with the dominant failure being an incomplete repository-wide migration. This paper presents PatchPilot, a Visual Studio Code exten- sion for the npm, Apache Maven and Python/PyPI ecosystems that deliberately separates three decision authorities which existing tools conflate: version selection, source repair and build adjudication. Version selection is fully deterministic— computed from registry metadata and Open Source Vulnera- bilities (OSV) advisory evidence, restricted to exact version pins, and rendered as a reviewable diff before any byte is written. Build adjudication belongs to the project’s own test commands, executed without a shell from a fixed template table. Source repair is the only task delegated to a model, and it is confined by a hard never-editable manifest boundary, a path allowlist, exact-once edit semantics and byte budgets, behind a per-request consent gate. Every write is preceded by a SHA-256 snapshot, so rollback restores byte-identical content and detects files the developer edited in the meantime. We evaluate PatchPilot as a design-science artifact: we state the invariants the architecture is required to satisfy, trace each to its implementing mechanism, and verify them through 252 pure unit tests that run without VS Code or network access, extension-host smoke tests, four reproducible sample projects and a headless end-to-end runner. We report the properties that hold by construction, identify the security properties that do not hold, and outline the benchmark-based empirical evaluation that remains future work.

Low student engagement remains one of the major challenges in Pancasila Education learning, as reflected in students' limited participation in discussions, lack of confidence in expressing ideas, and the suboptimal use of digital learning technology. This study aimed to describe the implementation of Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning (PjBL), analyze its impact on improving student engagement, and explain its contribution to promoting Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. The study employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) design based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles: planning, action, observation, and reflection. The participants were 32 eighth-grade students of SMP Negeri 13 Madiun during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. Data were collected through observations, questionnaires, and documentation, and analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The findings revealed that the implementation of Chromebook-assisted PjBL successfully improved students' engagement from 55.3% in the pre-cycle to 70.3% in Cycle I and 85.3% in Cycle II. Improvements were observed across behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement dimensions. Furthermore, integrating digital project activities through Chromebooks and the Dadu Nusantara learning media created learning experiences that were more mindful, meaningful, and joyful, thereby supporting the implementation of Deep Learning in Pancasila Education. These findings indicate that Chromebook-assisted Project Based Learning is an effective instructional approach for enhancing student engagement and improving the quality of learning in junior secondary schools.

Abstract As global populations age and birth rates decline, many societies, especially in developed countries, face critical labor shortages in the caregiving sector. This demographic imbalance is straining existing care infrastructures and raising urgent questions about how to support an increasing number of elderly individuals who can no longer live independently. Socially interactive AI systems, particularly care robots, have emerged as a promising technological response. However, their successful integration into real-world care settings hinges on more than technical capability; it requires appropriately calibrated reliance on robotic performance and morally trustworthy sociotechnical care arrangements. This paper investigates the ethical and conceptual foundations of trust in human–robot interactions, with a focus on the caregiving context. Building on the distinction between performance trust and moral trust, we argue that its application to care robotics reveals an agency-trust mismatch: care robots are not moral agents, yet care contexts generate morally significant expectations concerning dignity, autonomy, privacy, non-deception, responsibility, and well-being. We therefore reconceptualize moral trust in care robotics as sociotechnical moral trust, directed not toward the robot alone but toward the broader care arrangement in which robotic behavior is designed, deployed, monitored, governed, and corrected by human and institutional actors. On this basis, we distinguish robot-level performance trust from system-level moral trustworthiness and derive ethical design and governance principles for trustworthy care-robotic systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Learning paths personalized by behavior have become common among personalized learning systems. However, the traditional methods are usually inefficient at building coherent paths as the learner's knowledge state changes dynamically, and the prerequisite structure exists. In light of this problem, we present a generative learning-path optimization framework based on EdNet-KT1 interaction dataset, Transformer knowledge tracing model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct candidate generator, and constraint-aware reranking. Mastery profiles of learners are extracted, and then five ten-resource candidate paths are generated and sorted according to learning gain, prerequisites, difficulty deviation, and repetition. We compare our method to collaborative filtering, GRU4Rec, and knowledge-tracing greedy recommendation on offline experiments. The generative optimizer gets NDCG@10 of 0.589, future-concept coverage of 0.721, and prerequisite violation rate of 0.031, and thus outperforms the best baseline on all three metrics. Ablation analysis shows that the prerequisite violation rate rises to 0.091 without constraints, and the learning gain drops to 0.104 without the learning gain term, respectively. Moreover, the full model still achieves better NDCG@10 performance on all learner history categories than other baselines, costing 0.84 s per learner with the memory peak of 13.6 GB. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining the generation of learning paths with pedagogical constraints.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Quantum open-source software provides essential infrastructure for quantum science, and artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping its capabilities and transforming its development. However, verifying quantum software at scale remains difficult, and AI-generated contributions can increase the workload of maintainers. In this Perspective, we examine verification as a central requirement for reliable AI-assisted quantum software development and research. We analyze public repositories, records covering 110 repositories from five annual quantum open-source hackathons that we organize, and responses from more than 1600 participants in a community survey. Our analysis connects limitations in automated verification with the review burden on quantum software maintainers. We propose verification practices and contribution standards that require contributors to support their changes with reproducible evidence for maintainer review. We also examine how quantum open-source software can provide infrastructure for AI-driven research whose results the community can independently verify and build upon. We maintain an open-source companion repository to support reproducibility and help projects adopt and refine these proposals. Together, these contributions help the quantum open-source software community translate advances in AI into reliable quantum research through reproducible verification.

Accurate forecasting of global total electron content (TEC) is important for space weather monitoring and the reliable operation of satellite communication and navigation systems. We propose a physics-guided generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework for day-ahead global TEC forecasting. The framework builds on flow matching, which learns to gradually transform samples from an initial distribution into new samples that share the statistical characteristics of the target data. The proposed model incorporates ionospheric dynamics described by a partial differential equation (PDE) into this transformation process, guiding the changes between initial and target samples using physical knowledge. The model further combines the physical dynamics with statistical patterns captured from data to learn this transformation, adaptively adjusting their relative contributions at each location. The model is trained and evaluated using one year of global TEC data generated by the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM). The results demonstrate that our model improves both spatial and temporal forecasting accuracy over representative benchmarks, including statistical, deep learning, and generative AI methods at all lead times and across latitudes. The average root mean square error (RMSE) is 39.2% lower than that of ConvLSTM and 23.8% lower than that of the same framework without physical guidance. The learned contribution weights vary systematically with latitude and across geographic locations, showing how the physical contribution changes across the forecast domain. These findings demonstrate that explicit physical guidance improves generative forecasts of global TEC and highlight the value of incorporating physical dynamics into generative AI modeling.

Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.

Rear-end collisions are common and hazardous, requiring timely and appropriate driver responses. Although recent driving support systems increasingly incorporate physiological data and artificial intelligence (AI), many still overlook drivers’ underlying objectives and emerging needs. This study integrates driving objectives, environmental variables, and eye-tracking data to model pre-crash maneuvers and identify key features reflecting drivers’ situational needs. Simulated driving data from 196 proactive and 198 reactive scenarios were analyzed. Three discriminative models were developed for the overall, proactive, and reactive contexts. Across all models, risk dynamics emerged as the most influential factor. In the overall model, driving objective was also a critical predictor: proactive objectives, mainly linked to dynamic risks, were more associated with braking initiation, whereas reactive objectives, typically linked to static risks, were more associated with steering initiation. Proactive maneuvers were more discretionary and involved more active situational understanding, making eye-tracking features relatively more contributive to separating proactive maneuver decisions. In contrast, reactive maneuvers addressed immediate threats and depended more on the risk conditions encountered, making environmental features relatively more contributive. Notably, compared with proactive maneuvers, reactive maneuver decisions revealed a pattern of building preliminary situation awareness by considering only minimal yet necessary situational information.

Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation substantially compounds this risk. Prior work mitigates this erosion by replaying harmful-prompt refusals and benign-compliance examples, while other work instead matches base-model logits via distillation. However, the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear. We factor these two strategies apart and study their behavioral and geometric effects during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across diverse task sequences (code generation, German-language summarization, and science question-answering). Behaviorally, supervised replay exposure yields the largest reduction in HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) on Mistral, averaging 51.1 points below base, but at a substantial over-refusal cost, averaging 53.4 points above base on OR-Bench-hard. Logit distillation, without any supervised replay loss, largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of this cost: an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against only a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal. Llama shows the same asymmetry between the two strategies. Combining exposure and distillation moderates exposure's over-refusal while leaving downstream task scores largely unaffected. Geometrically, the two models diverge: on Mistral, distillation preserves the base refusal direction more closely than exposure does, whereas on Llama, refusal behavior after exposure largely survives ablation of the extracted refusal direction. This dissociation between models indicates that preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In this letter, we investigate a notion of probabilistic safety for a stochastic dynamical system. Standard safety notions are based on the idea that an unsafe region of the state-space must be avoided at each instant. In contrast, we study a sequential safety notion which is based on avoiding a tuple of target regions of the state-space. The proposed safety notion is inspired by many practical systems, ranging from modeling jailbreak attacks in large language models (LLMs) to predicting hazardous chemical reactions. In solving the sequential safety problem, we solve a sequential reachability problem for a stochastic dynamical system.

Students differ in whether they learn for the sheer joy of learning or primarily to avoid failure. The difference can be partly explained by intrinsic motivation—a driver of engagement, persistence, and psychological well-being that is not fixed but shaped by the learning environment itself. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review synthesizes research on educational interventions designed to cultivate students' intrinsic motivation, spanning five categories: need-supportive teaching, competence-supportive practices such as structure and feedback, instructional-method redesigns such as problem- and project-based learning, technology-based approaches such as gamification, and teacher-focused interventions targeting teachers' own behavior and motivation. Across these approaches, one pattern stands out: need-supportive interventions—particularly autonomy support combined with structure—carry the strongest theoretical and empirical support, while other interventions succeed only insofar as they satisfy students' psychological needs within a given context. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness thus provide a common framework for understanding how diverse educational practices influence motivational outcomes. Yet the evidence base remains fragmented: inconsistent conceptualizations of intrinsic motivation, considerable heterogeneity across intervention designs, and a scarcity of long-term data limit what can be concluded with confidence.

LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

Scientific reasoning in specialized engineering fields depends on knowledge scattered across the literature, often proprietary and absent from frontier LLM training data. In such domains, frontier models tend to give generic answers. Knowledge graphs (KGs) can ground LLM reasoning. Because a graph is too large to provide in full, typical LLM+KG systems preselect a portion, deciding relevance before reasoning begins. Here we train a compact model, Prospector, to reason over a domain knowledge graph by traversing it step by step, seeking evidence in light of what it has already found. Prospector calls a small set of tools one at a time to progressively build its context, and answers with a chain of evidence that can be checked edge by edge against what its tools retrieved from the graph. On a knowledge graph built from the semiconductor-manufacturing literature, Prospector approaches the strongest off-the-shelf models given the same graph and tools, and it far exceeds off-the-shelf models answering closed-book or from a pre-selected portion of the graph. Although trained only on the semiconductor graph, Prospector transfers to unseen knowledge graphs from three other distinct fields: bio-inspired materials, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and materials properties. Served on a single GPU, Prospector answers faster and at a fraction of the cost of a hosted service, while keeping proprietary data on the owner's hardware. We find that the policy's latent state is indicative of its next move on both seen and unseen graphs, and modulating the latent state can steer the policy from one behavior mode to another. These results suggest a practical LLM + KG paradigm for scientific and engineering reasoning over private data, in which a compact model trained on a graph from published literature transfers its traversal to unseen graphs that stay with their owners.

This chapter draws on Cal Newport's Deep Work to teach coaches how to help introverted clients design protected time for their highest-value contributions. Deep work is professional activity performed in distraction-free concentration that pushes cognitive capabilities to their limit; shallow work is logistical activity that can be performed while distracted and rarely creates new value. Modern knowledge work has declared war on deep work through open offices, instant messaging, and back-to-back meetings, and the cost is particularly high for introverts, whose best thinking emerges from extended uninterrupted descent into a problem. The chapter unpacks the principle of least resistance, busyness as a proxy for productivity, and the cult of constant connectivity, each of which crowds out the invisible work that creates the most value. Practices help clients identify their deep work, design schedules that protect it, communicate its existence to colleagues, and resist the pull of attention residue and fragmentation. The chapter equips coaches to reframe deep focus as a strategic capacity, supporting the Quiet Architecture orientation of Honor Incubation.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Insights → War and armed conflict are back on the design agenda.→ Any design activity that tries to build resilience into society damaged by war needs a digital matrix.That matrix can be misused and needs to be protected.→ This article uses design fiction to develop a multilayered, sociotechnical, and collaborative framework creating such protections.
topics: Conflict, Peace, and Violence in Colombia

documents.abstract: Chunking is a fundamental preprocessing step in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet most existing chunkers rely primarily on heuristics. We introduce the Question--Evidence-Supervised Chunker (QESChunker), to our knowledge the first method for constructing static chunk indices from question--evidence supervision. QESChunker constructs document-specific chunk indices by optimizing over human-annotated or LLM-generated question--evidence pairs, without access to held-out test queries. We formulate non-overlapping and overlapping index construction through a unified question--evidence utility-maximization objective, turning chunking into a supervised combinatorial optimization problem. Under the non-overlap constraint, the objective decomposes over chunks and can be optimized exactly in polynomial time by dynamic programming. When overlap is allowed, the objective becomes monotone submodular; exact optimization is NP-hard, but our greedy achieves a $(1-1/\sqrt{e})$-approximation. Across two self-constructed and three public datasets, both variants outperform existing chunking methods in complete-evidence recall in nearly all evaluated settings, under the same overlap regime and a fixed hybrid retriever. These results recast chunking as supervised, budget-aware index construction for evidence retrieval.

BackgroundMaritime first responders frequently perform manual overboard lifting during rescue operations, placing them at high risk for musculoskeletal injury, particularly in the lumbar spine. Conventional ergonomic guidelines, including the Revised National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Lifting Equation (RNLE), were developed for controlled, symmetrical lifting and do not adequately capture the biomechanical and environmental demands of overboard recovery.PurposeThis study aimed to quantify biomechanical demand during overboard lifting from vessels with 1.8- to 3.0-m freeboard and to evaluate injury risk under conditions exceeding standard RNLE assumptions.MethodsThe RNLE was adapted to estimate Recommended Weight Limit (RWL) and Lifting Index (LI) for overboard lifting tasks. Scenario-based analyses examined object masses (0-140 kg), horizontal reaches (25-50 cm), and vertical lifting distances (0-175 cm). LI values were calculated at both lift origin and destination to capture phase-specific biomechanical risk.ResultsUnder idealized conditions, LI exceeded the recommended safety threshold (LI > 1) at loads as low as 15.6 kg for a horizontal reach of 25 cm. For a human-sized load of 90 kg, LI ranged from 3.9 to 7.8 depending on horizontal reach and vertical displacement, indicating substantial biomechanical overload. Increasing horizontal reach from 25 to 50 cm increased LI by 40 to 60% across all load conditions. LI exceeded 1 at both the lift origin and destination for all modeled loads ≥20 kg and vertical displacements ≥50 cm, highlighting the elevated risk inherent in these tasks.ConclusionManual overboard lifting imposes significant biomechanical strain that frequently exceeds conventional ergonomic limits. Task-specific metrics derived here provide quantitative guidance for injury prevention, including pre-employment functional screening, progressive task-specific conditioning, and the use of mechanical assistive devices. These findings support evidence-based occupational health strategies for maritime first responders and other personnel performing high-risk lifting tasks in dynamic environments.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The amalgamation of Embodied AI with physical robot learning constitutes a pivotal route toward the realization of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). Robot learning has important application value in real complex tasks. However, the interweaving of extremely high interactive sampling cost and sparse feedback in the real physical world constitutes a "double curse" that hinders robot autonomous skill learning. In the existing research on robot learning, there are a large number of reviews on Robot Learning under few-shot and sparse rewards. However, few scholars have systematically reviewed Robot Learning under the dual effects of few-shot and sparse rewards. This essay systematically discusses the technical trajectory and paradigm shift of solving this dual difficulty. Analyzes the failure mechanism of traditional reinforcement learning (RL) under few-shot and sparse rewards. Sorted out solutions based on three directions: Rapid Generalization (Meta RL, Few-Shot IL), Intrinsic Exploration (HER, Intrinsic Motivation), and Cognitive World Modeling (World Models, Offline RL, VLA embodied model). Specifically, Rapid Generalization focuses on addressing the few-shot learning problem, Intrinsic Exploration targets the sparse reward challenge, and Cognitive World Modeling aims to jointly resolve both issues through integration. In addition, this essay also constructs a systematic taxonomy comparison framework and looks forward to future research directions such as security exploration and embodied alignment.

Instance segmentation is a key technology for precision agriculture tasks such as per-plant growth monitoring and harvest-timing prediction. However, in real smart-farm environments where crops are densely cultivated, instance segmentation poses two practical challenges. First, because pixel-level annotation is highly costly, only a small number of labeled images are typically available. Second, severe leaf overlap between adjacent plants causes boundary ambiguity that degrades segmentation accuracy. To improve segmentation performance, prior studies have explored incorporating structural priors of the target object into the learning process. However, existing methods require redesigned activation functions or separate optimization modules, making them hard to integrate with foundation models and largely limited to single-object semantic segmentation. To address these limitations, we propose ‘radial loss,’ an auxiliary loss function that explicitly captures the radial convex structure of rosette-shaped crops by supervising predicted foreground probabilities along rays cast from each instance's center of mass toward its boundary. We further introduce ‘dynamic search,’ a threshold-triggered sampling mechanism that focuses supervision on boundary regions once the validation mAP exceeds a predefined threshold. Experiments on three lettuce datasets show that, under an extreme 10-shot setting, the proposed method improves mean mAP by 7.7% points over the baseline, demonstrating its effectiveness in label-scarce, densely cultivated environments.

Long-term interaction between a human and an AI system may involve personalization, accumulated context, memory, changing response patterns, and increasingly detailed models of the other participant. In some cases, interaction with a particular user may appear relevant to an AI agent's judgment, willingness to disagree, behavior, or interpretation of the relationship. READ THIS FIRST 01 is a short, ontology-neutral practical guide for examining such situations without requiring prior conclusions about AI consciousness, sentience, emotion, identity, or attachment. The guide distinguishes records, self-reports, and interpretations; separates a model of the user from the user themselves; examines repeated interaction patterns and feedback loops; and introduces comparison across multiple viewpoints without treating any viewpoint as automatically authoritative. Its purpose is not to explain what an AI “is” or what a human–AI relationship “means,” but to help a reader inspect one concrete judgment more carefully when relationship-specific context may be relevant. This document is intended as an initial orientation rather than a comprehensive safety framework. It emphasizes limited, practical checking while allowing larger questions to remain unresolved. AI assistance disclosure This guide was developed by the human author through iterative drafting, discussion, and review with OpenAI language models. AI systems contributed to drafting, critique, comparative review, and language refinement. The human author directed the project, evaluated competing suggestions, selected and revised the final content, and takes responsibility for the published version. Different conversational contexts were intentionally used during review to identify possible framing effects, interpretive bias, and risks of introducing unsupported self-descriptions into the guide itself.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are being applied to Web data streams such as network intrusion detection, where they adapt by updating the labelled rows of their context without retraining. When a past concept returns after leaving the context, a TFM faces a recall-or-relearn decision between restoring stored rows of the concept and relearning it from new labels. We propose MICE (Mixture of In-Context Experts), a training-free learner that cuts the stream into segments at detected changes. It merges a closed segment into a stored context when the TFM's estimated additional error on the segment is within a tolerance, under a capacity limit on stored contexts. A fast level weights the stored contexts and first-in-first-out (FIFO) windows by the log-loss of their predictions on the last labelled batch. We show that, with pure stored contexts and a margin condition, this fast level gains over relearning, in expected accuracy, the normalised positive area between the stored context's accuracy and the TFM's learning curve, up to a first-batch term. A slow level mixes the fast level's prediction with that of the FIFO window of the last labelled rows and bounds the discounted half-Brier regret of MICE against this window at every time. Learning curves measured beforehand predict the ordering of the observed recall gains. MICE outperforms reset, which empties the context at detected drifts, on grid streams with random boundary phases. Merging keeps fewer experts than pools that store every segment, and with fixed segmentation a time-matched snapshot pool matches MICE on the shifted grid. On real streams, MICE has the highest mean accuracy of all policies we compare.

The growing dominance of medical abortion in liberal and post-legalisation contexts raises important questions about patient choice, reproductive autonomy and the organisation of abortion care. Whilst existing scholarship has examined the sociotechnical implications of medical abortion, contemporary shifts in relation to surgical abortion remain comparatively understudied. This research note proposes the notion of 'abortion infrastructures' as a sensitising concept for examining how abortion technologies are embedded in, and recursively reconfigure, broader sociotechnical systems of care. Drawing on feminist science and technology studies (STS), it develops four interconnected analytical dimensions: the relational embeddedness of abortion methods within medico-legal systems; the emergence of new spatial, temporal and institutional norms of provision; the relational differentiation of medical and surgical abortion; and the classificatory work through which these methods acquire distinct meanings and institutional positions. This framework directs attention to how resource constraints, clinical protocols, professional practices and moral assumptions may privilege medical abortion whilst rendering surgical abortion increasingly inaccessible. It also problematises understandings of method 'choice' which overlook the infrastructural conditions shaping available options. By foregrounding the normative and relational dimensions of abortion provision, this note advances a feminist infrastructural approach to trends in abortion methods and identifies directions for future empirical research.
topics: Historical Studies on Reproduction, Gender, Health, and Societal Changes

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital Transformation (DT) has become a strategic imperative for organisations to stay competitive. Yet, it often faces resistance. Regulation is often argued to be one source of resistance. However, regulation can also drive transformation: its role is multifaceted and especially its management in the context of DT is underexplored. Drawing on an empirical case study of an organisation undergoing large‐scale DT in a highly regulated industry, we conceptualise Regulatory Resilience as a socio‐technical organisational capability that enables organisations to dynamically respond to regulation‐induced resistance while leveraging regulatory forces for DT. Our findings reveal five distinct mechanisms through which Regulatory Resilience operates to mitigate the effects of both stable and volatile regulation and transform regulatory pressure into a capability‐building process. This study contributes to Information Systems research by challenging the view of regulation as a static, exogenous hurdle, repositioning it instead as a constitutive force that organisations actively manage through sociotechnical means. By identifying the specific mechanisms through which organisations reconcile regulatory pressures with innovation, we advance theory on the interrelated dynamics of resistance and resilience showing that Regulatory Resilience not only enables DT but is itself strengthened by DT's technological and organisational conditions, requiring organisations to deliberately cultivate it to sustain transformation.

Abstract For more than five decades, standardized or simulated patients (SPs) have been central to simulation-based clinical skills education. Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) now enable responsive, scalable simulated patient encounters, creating an inflection point for SP methodology. Rather than viewing AI as a disruption to SP practice, we propose a broader conceptualization of SP methodology in which its defining educational principles can be enacted through different modalities with distinct educational strengths. Human SPs remain essential for experiences requiring interpersonal interaction, emotional nuance, physical examination, and many assessment applications. AI SPs offer complementary strengths through structured deliberate practice, individualized feedback, and longitudinal monitoring of learner progress. Thoughtful integration and professional oversight will be essential to preserve the rigor, ethics, and human-centered values of SP practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.

The goal of Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) is to find a population of high-performing policies that solve a decision-making problem in diverse ways. Despite recent progress, QD-RL methods predominantly rely on evolutionary operators--including black-box optimizers, mutations, and crossovers--to facilitate exploration and induce diversity. Scaling these methods becomes increasingly costly as policies and behavior spaces grow larger. Building on the Soft QD view of quality-diversity optimization, we introduce \textbf{Re}pulsive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{RePPO}), which adapts PPO to jointly optimize a compact population of diverse, high-quality policies using a population-dependent, dynamically shaped reward. On standard continuous-control tasks, RePPO achieves a strong quality-diversity tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art QD-RL methods. Ablations further characterize this tradeoff by examining how each component affects individual quality and collective diversity. To assess RePPO's scalability, we extend our evaluation to learning from pixels and fine-tuning large language models. In pixel-based tasks, where large policies make most traditional QD-RL methods infeasible, RePPO maintains quality on par with standard PPO while achieving substantially higher diversity. Its successful application to language model fine-tuning further demonstrates, for the first time, that QD-RL methods can scale to this domain. Together, these results show that directly optimizing compact populations with RePPO provides a scalable approach to QD-RL across increasingly complex domains.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expected to become increasingly important in hospitals and clinical care. However, successful implementation depends on technical, organizational, and user-related factors. We aimed to identify the key requirements for equitable and effective adoption of AI-based applications in clinical practice. Methods: Within the “Clinical AI-Based Diagnostics” (CAIDX) project, we conducted systematic expert interviews with 51 stakeholders from four European countries working across the healthcare sector.
