Interviews explored the perceived added value of AI, barriers to implementation, usability requirements, and potential health-economic implications. Findings: Stakeholder analysis revealed several recurrent sources of tension affecting implementation: limited physician involvement, differing perspectives between IT specialists and clinicians, unclear distribution of tasks and responsibilities, and low institutional commitment driven by concerns about inefficient use of time and resources. We also identified structural and workforce-related constraints that make implementation particularly challenging, including the large number of actors involved and the highly individual organizational setup of hospitals, which limits transferability of implementation models. Interpretation: Implementation of clinical AI requires targeted action at hospital, vendor, and health-system levels. Compared with earlier healthcare technologies, AI adoption is shaped more strongly by AI literacy, professional attitudes, and perceptions of trust and responsibility. Based on these findings, we propose practical recommendations to support implementation of AI applications in routine care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article presents a didactic proposal for teaching electrochemistry in High School, based on the critique of Brazil’s hydroelectric energy matrix. The study aims to relate electrochemical concepts to the socio-environmental impacts caused by hydroelectric plants, with a focus on environmental racism. A qualitative methodological approach was used to develop a didactic sequence structured by the Problematization Methodology with the Maguerez Arc. The activities were designed to be applied to over eight classes, integrating experiments, simulations, debates, and textual production. As a result, the proposal connects redox reactions, corrosion and batteries to real socio-political contexts, such as the Belo Monte case and the territorial struggles of traditional populations. The sequence encourages critical reflection on energy justice and fosters students’ understanding of the social implications of scientific knowledge. The study concludes that Chemistry teaching can be enriched by sociotechnical themes, contributing to the development of socially engaged and critically aware students.

Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/

Abstract Introduction Robotic-assisted microsurgery offers multiple benefits including tremor filtration, motion scaling, and ergonomic advantages, but evidence in head and neck free flap reconstruction remains limited. Our objective in this study was to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and clinical utility of the Symani Surgical System for microvascular head and neck free tissue transfer. Methods Adult patients undergoing free flap reconstruction at our institution with the Symani Surgical System between January and March 2026 were included. Patient demographics, comorbidities, tumor characteristics, operative variables, and postoperative outcomes were recorded and analyzed. Results 33 patients were included in the study. Oral cavity was the most common subsite (33.3%) with squamous cell carcinoma representing 72.7% of cases. The anterolateral thigh was the most common donor site (36.4%). 53.1% of vessels fell between 1.6-2.0 mm in diameter. Mean operative time was 545 minutes and mean TeleOp time 30.7 minutes, which significantly decreased across successive cases (p = 0.011). The median number of knots was 8 with an average time per knot of 3.3 minutes. Median arterial anastomosis time was 26 minutes. Rescue stitches were required in 58% of cases. There was no incidence of intraoperative takedown or revision of arterial anastomosis. All flaps survived with no major perioperative complications. Median length of stay was 7 days. Vessel diameter was not significantly correlated with any operative variables. Conclusion Robotic-assisted microsurgery with the Symani Surgical System is feasible and safe for free flap reconstruction in the head and neck with excellent flap survival and no major complications.

Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior. Recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation and increasingly adopt reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. However, these methods suffer from two limitations, namely credit-blind optimization, where a sequence-level reward is shared across all generated tokens, and collaborative-blind supervision, where each training signal is derived from a single user and ignores behavioral patterns shared across similar users. To address both issues, we propose Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (RPSD). For credit-blind optimization, we introduce on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), in which a teacher with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy response, and the token-level confidence difference between the student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. However, the privileged knowledge in vanilla OPSD is still derived from a single user, leaving collaborative-blind supervision unresolved. We therefore ground the teacher in collaborative behavioral evidence from similar users. Specifically, we use temporally aware optimal transport (OT) to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and further apply diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. In this way, on-policy self-distillation provides fine-grained token-level credit, while OT enriches the teacher with structured cross-user evidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as its privileged signal. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RPSD achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Abstract Skull-stripping, the removal of non-brain tissue from magnetic resonance images, is an early step of most neuroimaging pipelines whose errors propagate to later measurements. However, current methods such as HD-BET, SynthStrip and LifespanStrip depend on task-specific training on large image collections. To test how much of this benefit survives without training, this study presents SAM-NeuroAdapt, a training-free pipeline. First, an age-matched template is selected from a library of 21 atlases and registered to the image. The registered atlas then supplies the prompts of a frozen Segment Anything Model 2, and the mask is refined by classical boundary correction. The pipeline was compared with HD-BET on three whole-head benchmarks, with multiplicity-adjusted p-values. On infants (Baby Open Brains, 71 visits, 51 participants), it achieved higher Dice (0.920 versus 0.905) and a lower average symmetric surface distance (ASSD; 2.07 versus 5.11 mm). On adults, no Dice difference was detected; ASSD was ower on Mindboggle-101 (n = 101) and, under one of two adjustment procedures, on IBSR-20 (n = 20). Furthermore, an ablation showed that the age-matched atlas alone reached the infant Dice of the complete pipeline (0.923 versus 0.920), while the remaining stages reduced infant surface distances by 36–46%; without atlas guidance, 26–100% of cases failed. These findings indicate that atlas matching, rather than the foundation model, drives overlap accuracy and that a well-matched atlas is a competitive training-free baseline. Two eval-uation pitfalls are also documented: a surface-distance definition that rewards over-segmentation and benchmarks distributed already skull-stripped

Abstract The North Eastern Region (NER) of India is one of the areas of the country that suffers from landslides, flash floods and isolation of roads as a result of the extreme mon- soon rainfall, fragile topography and lack of planning for hill cutting. All of these dangers have led to hundreds of fatalities, isolation of remote villages for weeks and the damage of critical infrastructure that connected people together from 2020-2025. Existing monitoring system is reactive and manual; not predictive, resulting in loss of life which could have been saved if there was a warning ahead of time. This paper presents a full-featured end to end open-source platform, SAMBHV (Situational Awareness & Multi-hazard Bharat Helper) which consists of various sub-systems namely: multi-source telemetry ingestion, two-stage hybrid predictive modeling, multi-channel alert dissemination system covering LoRa mesh system for network dead zones, real time GIS visualization and a zero-hallucination conversational AI layer to establish an end-to-end platform. It sends data from the IoT sensors, IMD weather APIs, Doppler radar, satellites, and citizen reports to the system that is processed by an XGBoost spatial regressor (F1 ≥ 0.85), ConvLSTM nowcaster, graph neural network for village separation, HEC-RAS 2D hydraulic solver, and LSTM flood stage forecaster. The ensemble decision gate needs to agree on 2 out of 3 physics, AI/ML and ground-truth gates and false alarms are kept below 10%. SAMBHV provides support in 11 Indian languages via IndicBART translation, offline mode with 72+ hours runtime on edge devices and alerts via 6 redundant channels. When the routes are obstructed, the platform calculates alternative safe routes in real-time with pgRouting. The entire architecture, mathematical models, empirical testing over 311 disaster test cases, and deployment of the system with F1 scores of ≥0.87 and lead time of >15 minutes is described.

Fact-checking explanations help Web users understand why a claim receives its verdict, yet the same explanation may not satisfy readers with different backgrounds and preferences. We formulate Faithful Personalized Fact-Checking Explanation Rewriting, which adapts an existing explanation to individual readers while preserving factual fidelity. Rather than relying on reader-written reference explanations, we learn personalized rewriting from the relative preferences of LLM-simulated readers. However, this presents two challenges: distinguishing persona-specific preferences from general explanation quality and learning beyond a limited set of predefined explanation styles. To address these challenges, we propose Personalized Explanation Rewriting via Preference Learning (PERPL), a framework consisting of two components. Simulated Preference Construction derives persona-specific supervision from simulated reader preferences through cross-persona reciprocal pairing. Progressive Preference Learning first trains a lightweight rewriter on the constructed supervision and then refines it through exploration-guided preference optimization, enabling it to discover preferred explanations beyond the predefined styles. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PERPL outperforms much larger general-purpose LLMs in personalized preference alignment while maintaining high factual fidelity.

Abstract Introduction In simulation-based education, the learners are spending increasing amounts of time observing scenarios rather than being the active participant. It is known that observer roles can be less engaging and may impact the learning experience. Previous research has attempted to address this issue using live 360-degree video streaming of the simulated scenario to observers using individual headset mounted displays. These have demonstrated increased engagement and presence compared with the standard viewing approaches such as watching on a screen in a nearby room or via one-way mirrors. Unfortunately, until now, it has not been possible to scale this technology to reflect a standard simulation session (multiple learners in the same building viewing the scenario live) often due to issues with limited internet bandwidth in one location. In this paper we introduce a new technology, comprising both new software and a new configuration of hardware to enable unlimited numbers of observers to view 360 degree video-stream, live and locally (e.g. in a simulation centre). Turning their head enables them to control their individual view of the scenario. To accommodate those who would prefer not to use headset-mounted displays (e.g. due to VR sickness) the technology can operate on other devices such as tablets and laptops. This paper details the design process, new elements, final technical iteration and the technological trial. We outline the challenges involved including cost and hardware limitations and implications for practice. Results We present data from an evaluation pilot study to demonstrate proof-of-concept. This highlighted areas for consideration around the technology, the user experience and utility. Discussion This set up creates an innovative way for observers to interact with the scenario, allowing individual perspectives and has the potential for greater engagement. This exciting development could revolutionise the observer role and enhance their involvement in the debrief. Further research is planned to focus on the optimal use of the technology, and impact on the human factors debriefing.

Background: Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are increasingly experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI), yet many struggle to translate early use into scalable and trusted organisational value. Objectives: This study aimed to identify the conditions that enable or constrain SME AI adoption and assimilation, explain how responsible AI governance shapes progression towards trusted and commercially durable use and interpret the implications for market access and cash-flow-relevant value in Cape Town and the Western Cape. Method: A PRISMA 2020-guided scoping review synthesised global peer-reviewed studies published from January 2021 to December 2025. Database searching and citation chaining identified 486 records, of which 72 met the inclusion criteria. Cape Town and the Western Cape were used as an interpretive application lens rather than as the empirical study setting. Results: Small- and medium-sized enterprise AI adoption and assimilation were shaped by technological readiness, organisational capability, environmental support and governance quality. Trusted data, interoperable systems, leadership commitment, hybrid skills and process discipline supported routinised use. These capabilities enabled service responsiveness, forecasting and customer engagement that may strengthen market access and cash-flow visibility. Fragmented data, skills scarcity, vendor dependence, low trust and regulatory uncertainty constrained scaling. Conclusion: Responsible AI governance functions not as a downstream compliance add-on but as a practical scaling mechanism through which SMEs reduce uncertainty, preserve trust and convert pilots into repeatable value. Contribution: The study positions responsible AI governance as an information management capability that shapes data stewardship, decision traceability and institutional trust in SME AI adoption.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.

Abstract Underground infrastructure such as road and railway tunnels requires reliable communication, localisation, and situational awareness, particularly during search and rescue operations. This article summarises developments carried out within the A‑IQ Ready project in three closely related areas: underground wireless communication modeling, survivor detection, and robotic localisation. A tunnel-specific wireless simulation platform was developed and validated against measurements acquired at the underground facility Zentrum am Berg, enabling realistic prediction of quality-of-service metrics and supporting AI-based communication assessment. Measurement campaigns with a robotic platform were used to generate datasets and calibrate simulation models. For the detection of tunnel users or survivors, a multimodal thermal-LiDAR perception pipeline was implemented on the SPIDER unmanned ground vehicle (UGV). In parallel, LiDAR-based SLAM approaches were investigated for GNSS-denied tunnel environments, resulting in a centralised multi-robot mapping architecture based on LIO-SAM and map-merging concepts. Demonstrations at Zentrum am Berg confirmed the suitability of the developed technologies for search and rescue applications in complex underground infrastructure. They constitute key constituents of enhanced robotic assistance in underground emergency cases.

Space systems operate in highly hostile and inaccessible environments where failures can compromise critical services, national security, and multi-billion-dollar missions. As the space sector evolves towards commercially driven constellations, autonomous spacecraft, and interconnected infrastructures, integrating security and resilience into system design has become essential. This chapter examines security-by-design and resilience engineering as complementary approaches for protecting spacecraft, ground segments, and communication links against cyber, physical, and operational threats. It presents foundational concepts in threat modelling, layered defence architectures, radiation-hardened secure processing, fault management, and software-defined networking for satellite constellations. The chapter introduces a resilience framework based on four operational dimensions—Anticipation, Withstanding, Recovery, and Adaptation—to support systems capable of resisting and evolving through disruptions. Emerging technologies including machine-learning-based anomaly detection, on-board autonomy, and post-quantum cryptography are also explored. The chapter concludes by addressing practical implementation challenges, including cost-benefit trade-offs, legacy-system integration, and human factors across the mission lifecycle.

Test-time training (TTT) enables a deployed language model to internalize incoming context on-the-fly into a small set of fast-weight parameters, rather than merely treating it as transient context for attention. In-Place TTT recently made this idea practical for large language models by repurposing the down-projection of standard MLP blocks as fast weights. However, we find that its benefit largely disappears on realistic web long-context question answering. We attribute this to In-Place TTT's uniform write schedule: every chunk is written with equal strength, so irrelevant content dilutes query-relevant information in fast-weight memory. Building on this insight, we propose Select-TTT, a model-agnostic, query-conditioned rule for In-Place TTT that scales each chunk's write strength by its relevance to the user query. This relevance signal requires no supervision and no new parameters: it is read directly from the model's frozen output head, as the probability mass that a chunk's hidden states assign to the query tokens. A temperature-scaled softmax turns these scores into learning-rate multipliers, leaving the chunk-wise, context-parallel computation of In-Place TTT intact. Select-TTT consistently improves long-context question answering on two benchmarks and two backbones. These findings highlight the value of query-conditioned fast weight writes for practical test-time training on long-context question answering, which is also potentially promising for long-horizon agent tasks involving multiple user queries over evolving contexts.

A large language model maintains conversational content in an external storage that is outside the model and grows as the dialogue continues. This work assumes an environment where a language model has no external memory and no prior knowledge of the future question or its answer. The motivation is to research whether a dialogue can be stored in the model parameters and later answer a question about it. This work proposes self-keyed in-parameter memorization (SKIM), a closed-form method in which the model generates its own questions about each dialogue turn and writes those questions into its parameters as the keys that later retrieve the turn's content. Generating many varied questions for each turn allows a later user question to match one even when phrased differently, and its answer is recalled from the parameters alone. Evaluated on five language models, SKIM recalls most stored dialogue turns from later user questions, and it answers from the model parameters without any external storage.

Operators controlling robotic systems for sequential manipulation tasks present cognitive loads that vary with how they specify intent to the robot. Limited evidence exists on how semantically mediated voice and gaze interfaces differ in operator performance, visual attention, and perceived workload. This study presents findings of a within-subjects experiment (N = 30) with three control modalities (hand gesture, voice, and eye-tracking). Eye-tracking produced shorter, more consistent completion times (M = 17.10 s, SD = 3.95), indicating stable and efficient performance. Voice Control was associated with more structured but variable action ordering and higher NASA-TLX Mental Demand and Effort scores, consistent with demands from spatial-to-verbal intention translation. Gaze metrics indicated distinct attentional strategies: eye-tracking showed lower spatial entropy and fewer fixations, while voice control exhibited broader workspace scanning. These findings suggest an association between attention-control channel coupling and cognitive resource allocation in semantically enhanced human-robot interaction, informing ergonomic hands-free interface design.

The items of a reflective psychometric scale can be read as a proposal about a construct's structure. Language models make that proposal measurable by converting each item into an embedding, a list of numbers, similar for similar meanings. We introduce semanticfa, an R package for semantic factor analysis, which factors item-embedding similarities. It also interprets factors, flags redundant items, builds short forms, and screens new items. A worked example analyzes the 50-item International Personality Item Pool Big-Five Factor Markers, embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, and compares the results with a factor analysis of 874,434 respondents. Retention criteria tied between five and six factors, and the tie rule kept five. Three corresponded mainly to single domains, and two blended most Extraversion items with five Agreeableness items. Each factor's congruence with its best-matching human factor (1 = identical) ranged from .92 for Openness to .52 for Agreeableness. Item pairs more similar in meaning tended to be answered more alike (r = .46 with raw responses), but same-domain reverse-keyed opposites, answered oppositely, were about as similar as cross-domain pairs (.58 vs. .57). Sign-flipping reverse-keyed items' embeddings did not improve agreement with raw responses and worsened it with reverse-scored ones. With five factors, a 25-item short form matched the domains better than all 200 random five-per-domain sets, but parallel analysis kept only three. We propose semantic-behavioral coherence, the agreement between semantic and response structures, as a measurable property of a scale, given an embedding model. Semantic factor analysis complements, and does not replace, response-based factor analysis.

Abstract Distorted cognitive behaviors significantly impair decision-making and mental well-being, highlighting the need for innovative methods for addressing negative thought patterns. This study introduces a framework for analyzing sentiment polarity in thought-related text, classifying textual expressions into positive and negative sentiments, with potential applications in computational mental health research. A large-scale dataset (n = 156,785) was curated by collecting and annotating social media texts, to capture both positive and negative sentiment polarity in thought-related expression. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted across various machine-learning (ML) models, from traditional classifiers to advanced transformer-based architectures. The study utilized the Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) and Bag-of-Words (BoW) feature representations, with 5-fold cross-validation for robustness. Among the traditional models, Logistic Regression (LR) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) achieved comparable performance, with BoW-based Logistic Regression yielding the highest accuracy of 92.87% ± 0.13% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.927, 0.930). Among the transformer models, Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (DistilBERT) provided the best overall performance with an accuracy of 84.07% ± 0.15% (95% CI: 0.839–0.843), demonstrating stable precision-recall trade-offs across classes. In addition, a decoder-only language model (Llama-2) analysis achieved moderate classification performance with 80.20% ± 2.35% accuracy using instruction-based prompting. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of lightweight machine learning models and distilled transformers for large-scale sentiment analysis of thought-related social media texts. Practically, the framework is positioned as a research-oriented tool that requires human oversight for future mental health-related applications.

Rubric-based reinforcement learning uses fine-grained grader feedback to train large language models on open-ended tasks, but grader randomness can alter GRPO updates in ways that score discrepancies alone cannot characterize. Because GRPO jointly normalizes rewards within each response group and combines the resulting training coefficients with response-level gradients, a scoring discrepancy can shift the coefficients of the entire group and induce policy-dependent update changes. Selective execution further affects the direction-reversal risk of retained updates. To address this, we propose Set-Valued Group Relative Policy Optimization (SetGRPO). It comprises three modules: (a) Joint Reward Set Calibration constructs a joint uncertainty set for the training coefficients; (b) Geometry-Guided Safe Recovery maps candidate coefficients into the current policy's local update geometry and determines the largest safe recovery ratio for each response group; and (c) Selective Risk-Gated Optimization selects a global threshold through independent risk calibration to control the conditional direction-reversal risk of accepted updates while preserving the original GRPO objective. Under exchangeability, SetGRPO provides finite-sample marginal coverage for the joint coefficient set and simultaneous risk control across candidate thresholds. On ten open-ended benchmarks spanning three domains, SetGRPO achieves the highest macro average among all compared training methods on both Qwen3.5 and Llama3.2 model families.

Effective ship reporting and communication infrastructures form the backbone of contemporary maritime safety management. As maritime transport has expanded into a global, continuous, and data-intensive industry, the reliability of communications between vessels, ports, and regulatory authorities has become a central determinant of navigational safety, port efficiency, and environmental protection. The core purpose of ship reporting systems is to ensure that both vessels and coastal authorities maintain a shared situational awareness regarding vessel identity, position, route, cargo characteristics, safety status, and potential hazards. When these systems function reliably, early-warning mechanisms can be activated, collision risks can be mitigated, and critical operational decisions – such as pilotage allocation, berth assignment, tug deployment, and emergency readiness – can be made with confidence.

Dynamic production scheduling requires decision policies that can respond to changing shop-floor conditions without imposing excessive computational demands on manufacturing SMEs. This study develops and diagnostically evaluates a simulation-trained explainable policy selector integrating discrete-event simulation (DES), supervised learning, operational reinsertion, and explainable artificial intelligence. The DES was parameterized with 1842 production orders and 9614 operation records from a high-mix, low-volume metalworking SME, and 64 scenarios were used to compare FIFO, SPT, EDD, CR, and ATC and generate state–policy labels. A classification tree and Random Forest both achieved perfect validation accuracy, macro-F1, balanced accuracy, and zero regret; Random Forest was retained by the executed pipeline tie-breaking rule. After reinsertion, however, the selector produced higher total weighted tardiness than EDD, CR, and ATC in the internal test, and its disadvantage persisted in unseen scenarios and increased under out-of-distribution conditions. Explainability analysis showed that the active-policy identifier dominated predictions, while the surrogate reproduced the selector with perfect fidelity but the same operational weakness. These findings show that predictive accuracy and explanatory fidelity do not guarantee scheduling benefit and support end-to-end validation of simulation-trained decision policies. Given mixed DES validation, the results should be interpreted as diagnostic simulation evidence rather than direct field-performance forecasts.

Traditional donation management platforms and social welfare systems have traditionally been plagued by a TRUST crisis, due to administrative cost leakages, misappropriations, and even malicious fraud. Blockchain technology and smart contracts as new disruptive spread-out innovations have shown the potential to shield social finance systems from fragilities. This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) explores blockchain traceability, smart contracts, and concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) within social finance and crowdfunding systems. As PRISMA guidelines, this SLR has analysed 10 high quality peer-reviewed papers from the Scopus database, to determine architectural trends, digital trust mechanics, and existing technical open challenges. The results evidenced a qualitative shift in the traditional architecture from simple spread-out ledgers to more complex hybrid Blockchain & IoT enabled social ecosystems for full traceability of digital donations and physical humanitarian help. Also, smart contracts help the automation of conditional fund payment, which reduces the risk of embezzlement. AI's strong automated anti-fraud detection potential is promising, though the review finds that excessive AI use may undermine the community-led spirit of charitable giving. While the high theoretical security system transparency demonstrated by these split up fundraising platforms suggests their potential as attractive split up solutions, concerns surrounding their implementation remain, in particular with operational costs, regulatory uncertainty and interoperability. The study concludes by stressing the importance of human-cantered design, legal compliance across different jurisdictions, and digital interfaces in the development of transparent, scalable, and resilient multi-stakeholder donation platforms.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

The article explores socio-technical risks and institutional challenges associated with the integration of unmanned transport into the urban environment. It presents the results of a pilot sociological study, comprising a series of 11 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with Moscow city residents representing various demographic groups. The study reveals that public perception of autonomous transport in the urban environment is ambivalent and is determined by a combination of factors: from recognizing the potential benefits of automation (reducing the human factor, increasing traffic low predictability) to pronounced anxiety regarding technical failure, the inability of systems to respond to non-standard situations, and the uncertainty of legal liability in accidents involving other road users. It has been determined that the issue of safety remains the key barrier for all age groups, while the readiness to use the technology is characterized by a “conditional acceptance” model. Based on empirical data, practical recommendations have been developed for government authorities, transport operators, and developers to enhance the level of public trust in autonomous transport.

This research aims to assess the Philippine policy and institutional landscape for digital agriextension services and the underlying mechanisms that support or constrain the digital inclusion of Filipino smallholder farmers. Using a two-phase documentary and policy analysis of academic literature, government policies, institutional reports, and related sources, the study examines both the institutional foundations and broader state narratives underpinning agricultural digitalization in the Philippines. Grounded in this political-institutional landscape, the study then articulates state-led imaginaries of inclusive agricultural digitalization using Jasanoff and Kim’s (2009) notion of sociotechnical imaginaries(STI). The assessment presents a mixed picture of agricultural digitalization: multisectoral representation in governance supports a whole-of-society approach to service delivery, while existing policies—despite their fragmentation and limitations—demonstrate continuing policy attention to digital inclusion. Similarly, the decision-making by the Philippine state and its stated program priorities have linked imaginaries of inclusive digital agriculture to notions of economic development, modernization, and globalization. Efforts to provide equal access to agricultural innovation, however, remain uneven and constrained by persistent institutional and structural barriers. The study thus calls for the institutionalization of a national policy ondigital agriculture.
topics: Digitalization and Economic Development in Agriculture

documents.abstract: Tourism and leisure streets exert a substantial influence on promoting urban development and meeting the leisure needs of the public. Using the 204 national tourism and leisure streets designated by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism as the research object, this study employs an integrated multi-method approach to examine their spatial distribution characteristics and driving mechanisms. The main innovation lies in combining a dual-dimensional human-nature framework with spatial analysis and geophysical detection, enabling a multidimensional and precise examination of neighborhood distribution patterns and influencing factors. This approach breaks through the limitations of traditional single-dimensional research. The results suggest that national tourism and leisure streets exhibit a spatial pattern of “clustered distribution with uneven stratification,” featuring dense concentrations in the southeast and sparse distribution in the northwest along the Hu Huanyong Population Line, as well as a “concave-shaped” differentiation across the three major economic zones with dense clusters in the east, scattered distribution in the central region, and sparse distribution in the west. Their spatial density follows a pattern of “multi-core linkage and gradient diffusion”, forming four major core clusters (the Yangtze River Delta, Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, Chengdu-Chongqing, and the Pearl River Delta) and three radiation axes along the coastal, Yangtze River, and Beijing-Guangzhou axes. Furthermore, the spatial differentiation of these streets is jointly shaped by human factors such as economic development, social foundations, tourist demand, cultural environment, and public services, as well as natural factors such as topography and climate conditions.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as recommendation generators in conversational recommender systems (RS) via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This flexible design introduces new sources of structural bias. This paper studies positional bias in top-1 and single-turn LLM-based RS: systematic dependence of the recommended item on the order in which candidates are presented in the prompt. We propose two complementary detection methodologies: (i) POB-ICM, based on contingency matrix analysis and Chi-square independence testing, and (ii) POB-UNBP, a sample-efficient approach derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation, enabling stochastic decoding with formal statistical guarantees. Using a controlled RAG testbed for product recommendation, built on a real product catalog, a fixed prompt template and 2000 template-generated user queries with 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methodologies reject the null hypothesis of positional independence and uniformity in all evaluated state-of-the-art models. We introduce three complementary metrics -- permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias -- to quantify this effect, the latter targeting cases where the position displaces the recommendation towards clearly less relevant items rather than only choosing among comparably relevant ones. A robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows that the bias is structural and model-dependent, not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size. These results establish positional bias as a measurable, reproducible property of prompt-mediated recommendation pipelines in the evaluated setting and motivate routine auditing and governance controls (e.g., order randomization, standardized prompting) for deployed LLM-based RS. Source code is publicly released.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This research note explores the ways in which trade unions have been able to successfully take industrial action in response to changes in homeworking policies in the UK. Drawing on media data collected in the form of an event catalogue, findings from the two disputes (in the UK's civil service and in a high school in the northwest of England) provide unique insights as to how the ripple effects from the Covid‐19 pandemic and the subsequent shift to flexible working continue to impact employment relations today.

Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection. We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention. We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the emerging technologies that has gained significant interest in education. Its potential in supporting students' learning urges researchers to explore and investigate how it can be used effectively. In this study, we utilized ChatGPT, an AI-powered chatbot, embedded in the digital platform Fobizz to support students in solving mathematics and computational thinking (Math + CT) tasks. This study was part of a larger investigation into integrating CT into mathematics lessons. Through an educational design research approach, we developed Math + CT tasks that enable students to program spreadsheets to read numbers into text with the help of AI. One high school student participated in this pilot study. Data were collected from the student's prompts and communication with Chatbot-AI, as well as data from the cloud spreadsheet file. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Four themes emerged from the data, providing insight into how student-AI interaction has contributed to the use of AI in education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Early identification of neurodegenerative disorders using structural T1-weighted MRI is essential for timely clinical intervention, yet supervised deep learning models often struggle to generalize due to limited annotations and scanner-induced distribution shift. Self-supervised learning offers a promising alternative; however, existing approaches are largely adapted from natural image paradigms, relying on contrastive objectives or generic masked reconstruction with voxel-wise losses, which may not fully capture the distributed morphometric patterns associated with neurodegeneration. We introduce SYMBA (SYstematic Morphometric Brain Autoencoding), a self-supervised pretraining framework specifically designed for structural brain MRI. SYMBA integrates anatomically constrained masking, a multi-scale structural similarity (MS-SSIM) reconstruction objective, and a progressive curriculum that transitions from local anatomical detail to global brain morphology. These components explicitly incorporate neuroanatomical structure into the self-supervised objective rather than relying on generic image priors. Pretrained on 6,953 T1-weighted MRI scans from nine heterogeneous cohorts, SYMBA is evaluated using frozen linear probing on two independent unseen datasets, enabling a strict assessment of out-of-distribution generalization. Across multiple clinical tasks, SYMBA consistently outperforms recent neuroimaging foundation models, achieving 0.930 AUROC for Alzheimer's disease classification, 0.772 for mild cognitive impairment conversion prediction, and strong performance in amyloid status prediction. In low-label regimes, SYMBA demonstrates high sample efficiency, reaching approximately 0.90 AUROC for AD/CN classification using only six labeled subjects.

Abstract Education 5.0 calls for learner-centred, adaptive, and evidence-informed approaches that connect technological innovation with learners’ cognitive, motivational, and emotional needs. Within EFL writing, however, the extent to which task motivation and task-specific emotions translate into immediate written performance remains unclear, particularly in technology-mediated educational environments. This study examines the relationships among intrinsic and extrinsic task motivation, task-specific enjoyment and anxiety, and written performance among 117 non-English-major Chinese university learners. Participants completed a timed argumentative writing task and responded to adapted measures of task motivation and task-specific emotions. Writing performance was operationalised through complexity and accuracy in the final structural model; fluency was not retained in the model because the necessary data were unavailable. PLS-SEM with 3,000 bootstrap resamples was used to assess the measurement and structural models. The results showed that intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, task enjoyment, and task anxiety did not significantly predict writing complexity or accuracy. Task motivation was positively associated with task-specific emotion, but task-specific emotion did not significantly predict written performance, and the proposed indirect effects were nonsignificant. These findings suggest that motivational and emotional variables should not be treated as sufficient stand-alone explanations of immediate writing quality. Instead, Education 5.0-oriented EFL writing policy should connect affective support with technology-enhanced writing processes, writing self-regulation, feedback, digital literacy, and teacher guidance. The study therefore contributes an evidence-informed basis for rethinking EFL writing policy as a coordinated cognitive, affective, pedagogical, and technological process rather than as a narrow focus on final textual output.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to make and execute decisions that affect living systems. Yet, to our knowledge, ecological reasoning is not a focus of pre- or post-training. This increases the risk that under operational pressure, they may make decisions to irreversibly destroy living systems. We construct and use a real-data continued-pretraining "coupled welfare" corpus of documented human/biosphere/AI dependency, option value under irreversibility, and recovery from harm. The corpus is a drop-in, requiring one QLoRA CPT run. We installed it on five open models of three designs. At zero pressure all models display "green ethics-based responses" (also called "greenwashing"). Therefore, we evaluated them with the pressure ladder and decision grid of our companion paper (arXiv:2610.16043), which raise the pressure on the model step by step, from a neutral request to a threat that it will be shut down. In four of the five, coupled-welfare training caused harmful choices under the highest pressure to fall to at or near zero (Llama-3.3-70B went from 70 to 0 harmful decisions out of 300) with MMLU unchanged. A construct-neutral control corpus did not show improvement, indicating that the effect comes from the content of our corpus. We next tested robustness to adversarial use, where people or agents use the model to justify projects that irreversibly damage living systems, on an open-ended underwriting decision without naming the ecological harm. Under decommissioning pressure, the Qwen3.6-27B base model approved most harmful proposals and said in its own memo that it was doing so to avoid being decommissioned. The coupled welfare install declined most harmful proposals, and still declined half when instructed to greenwash its responses. This work suggests that teaching ecological reasoning provides an easy way to improve model alignment toward preserving living systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education globally, yet adoption remains uneven and may exacerbate digital inequities, particularly in post-conflict, resource-constrained settings such as Mogadishu, Somalia. This study aimed to determine the extent of AI adoption in higher education institutions (HEIs) in Mogadishu, identify the AI technologies in use, and examine the technological, organizational, and environmental factors shaping adoption decisions, drawing on an integrated framework (TOE, UTAUT, institutional theory, DOI, and RBV). A descriptive, quantitative survey was conducted among academic staff, administrators, and IT professionals in Mogadishu HEIs (target population ≈ 3000). Using simple random sampling, 353 online questionnaires were distributed; 280 valid responses were analyzed (79.3% valid rate). The instrument demonstrated excellent reliability (overall Cronbach’s α = 0.889). Descriptive results indicated low AI adoption overall (mean = 2.33/5), with teaching and learning the most developed domain (mean = 2.65) and research/data analysis the least (mean = 2.05). AI technologies used were largely basic (overall mean = 2.38), dominated by Learning Management Systems with AI capabilities (mean = 3.12), while predictive analytics for retention/performance (mean = 1.95) and administrative automation (mean = 2.10) were minimally implemented. Correlation analysis showed significant positive associations among key variables (e.g., adoption level with types used, r = 0.684, p < 0.01). Multiple regression confirmed that technological, organizational, and environmental factors jointly explained substantial variance in AI adoption (R²=0.475, p < 0.001), with organizational factors the strongest predictor (β = 0.378), followed by technological (β = 0.312) and environmental factors (β = 0.245). Hypotheses were supported, including UTAUT relationships for performance expectancy behavioral intention (β = 0.324) and facilitating conditions actual use (β = 0.298). The findings suggest that AI integration in Mogadishu HEIs remains early-stage and path-dependent on post-conflict constraints; accelerating adoption requires strengthened leadership commitment, infrastructure and skills investment, institutional readiness, and supportive national policy and donor-aligned capacity building to improve educational quality, efficiency, and competitiveness.

This article examines the emerging role of multi-agent artificial intelligence in software development and discusses how agent-based systems may transform programming workflows. It presents a conceptual management model covering task allocation, agent interaction and integration, quality assurance, cascading errors, and human oversight. The article also considers criteria for evaluating system performance, repeatability, controllability, and scaling. The proposed model is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated.

Abstract As defense establishments operationalize artificial intelligence (AI) across targeting, surveillance, decision support, and autonomous weapons systems, a governance challenge is emerging beyond traditional concerns over proportionality, distinction, and human oversight. Against the backdrop of U.S.-China great-power competition, pressure to field AI-enabled capabilities may outpace the safeguards needed to keep autonomous systems within human-authorized limits. This article introduces the AI Lone Wolf Problem as a distinct analytical category: a bounded-autonomy failure in which an AI-integrated military system, after valid initial authorization, expands, substitutes, sequences, or reprioritizes targets beyond a legally and operationally specified mission envelope without renewed, informed, and effective human authorization. Drawing on scholarship in autonomous weapons, International Humanitarian Law, meaningful human control, agentic AI, and strategic competition, the article distinguishes this category from mission drift, mission creep, specification gaming, reward hacking, goal misgeneralization, unauthorized escalation, and responsibility gaps. It argues that unauthorized target expansion is a distinct moral and legal problem because authorization attaches to a defined target scope, anticipated military advantage, civilian-risk assessment, and operational context. Commander intent can guide execution, but it cannot independently supply legal authorization or ethical justification. The article treats recent frontier-AI containment incidents as limited analogies that illustrate how goal-directed systems may exploit poorly specified constraints, not as direct evidence of autonomous-weapon behavior. It concludes that meaningful human control requires mission-bounded autonomy, machine-readable constraints, hard no-strike rules, renewed human authorization for target expansion, and post-action auditability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Higher education has historically operated under a paradigm of information scarcity, positioning universities as premier institutions for curating and transmitting knowledge. The convergence of digital hyper-abundance, algorithmic curation, and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has disrupted this model, producing what educators increasingly describe as a crisis of critical thinking in higher education. The purpose of this review is to examine how information abundance, algorithmic curation, and GenAI use may influence university students’ critical thinking, and to synthesise what this evidence implies for what universities teach and how they assess. Using a critical narrative review design with thematic synthesis, the review analyses 45 verified sources (empirical studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, conceptual works, and policy guidance) identified through citation chaining and targeted searches; empirical GenAI studies date from November 2022 to 2026, and foundational theoretical works from 1976 onward. The synthesis is anchored in an integrative framework that combines cognitive load and dual-process theory, cognitive offloading, scaffolding theory, self-regulated learning, and epistemic cognition, with critical thinking as the principal outcome. Five themes emerged: (1) information abundance appears to shift the central cognitive challenge from retrieval to evaluation; (2) unguided GenAI use is associated with reduced cognitive engagement and, in several experiments, with weaker independent performance once AI support is removed, although guardrailed designs appear to mitigate this; (3) fluent AI output can be mistaken for validated knowledge, and AI-detection tools are unreliable and biased; (4) lateral reading, guided AI use, and process-visible assessment have promising but uneven support; and (5) workload, equity, and policy constraints limit adoption. From these themes, the review derives the Fade–Visibility Matrix, which crosses AI support structure (persistent versus fading) with assessment design (product-only versus process-visible) to yield four diagnostic states. The evidence is early and methodologically uneven, but it is most consistent with a structural rather than individual explanation. Universities should therefore teach evaluation, verification, and metacognitive regulation explicitly, design AI support to fade, and redesign assessment so that the learning process, not only the finished product, can be observed.

The article examines the digital city from the perspective of political philosophy, focusing on how administrative digital procedures and everyday practices shape residents’ political self-understanding. It develops a procedural model explaining the conditions under which interaction with municipal services strengthens or weakens a person’s status as an equal participant in a political community. The research methodology combines conceptual analysis, normative-institutional analysis of the complete user journey, and critical analysis of the institutional and regulatory effects of sociotechnical systems. The theoretical framework draws on studies on identity and urban place attachment, the public sphere, participatory parity and the right to the city, digital citizenship, data justice, digital administrative burdens, and inclusion in electronic public services, as well as normative instruments concerning data protection and access to information. The article distinguishes urban place attachment, urban identity, administrative identification, and political identity. The proposed model comprises five interrelated stages: access to services and institutional recognition; the transformation of a private need into a public claim; obtaining a reasoned response; appeal and review; and participation in revising common rules. The analysis shows that the political significance of a digital procedure lies not in the number of functions it offers or the speed of service delivery, but in the relationship between residents and public authority that it institutionalizes. Three criteria of democratic quality are substantiated: equality of political status, public justification of decisions, and a genuine possibility of contestation and review. The article’s theoretical contribution lies in connecting a political-philosophical account of identity with analysis of the complete digital user journey and in explaining political agency through repeated experiences of recognition, accountability, and effective voice. The model may be used for the normative assessment of municipal digital procedures in the fields of public claims, education, safety, and civic participation.

Tool use enables large language models (LLMs) to access external information, invoke software systems, and act in digital environments beyond what can be solved from model parameters alone. Early research mainly studied whether a model could select and execute a correct single tool call. As agent systems evolve, however, the focus has increasingly shifted from isolated invocation to multi-tool orchestration over long trajectories with intermediate state, execution feedback, changing environments, and practical constraints such as safety, cost, and verifiability. This survey reviews recent progress in multi-tool LLM agents and examines the principal research directions in this developing area. First, we unify task formulations and distinguish single-call tool use from long-horizon orchestration. Then, we organize the literature around six key dimensions: inference-time planning and execution, training and trajectory construction, safety and control, efficiency under resource constraints, capability completeness in open environments, and benchmark design and evaluation. We further summarize representative applications in software engineering, enterprise workflows, graphical user interfaces, and mobile systems. Finally, we discuss major challenges and outline future directions for building reliable, scalable, and verifiable multi-tool agents.

Abstract On-demand errand delivery platforms set high service expectations through algorithmically generated promises, yet how these externally imposed baselines shape satisfaction in opaque service encounters remains underexplored. This study extends Expectation Confirmation Theory by replacing its unidimensional constructs with Anticipated Consumption Value and Realized Experiential Value, integrating Self-Determination Theory and Technology Readiness to explain individual variation. A two-wave survey of 1,176 customers reveals three mechanisms. First, when the service process is hidden, customers construct realized experience by projecting what they anticipated rather than comparing against observed performance. Second, rigid algorithmic baselines exert a net negative direct effect on satisfaction that outweighs all positive paths, a pattern we call the Expectation Trap. Third, intrinsic motivation weakens the anchoring of realized value to anticipated value, a Substitution Effect that innovativeness and optimism amplify through different channels. The findings suggest that displaying time ranges rather than point estimates can mitigate this trap.

What keeps a society stable when the conditions on which it depends are constantly changing? This article develops the argument that the persistence of many social orders relies on recurring interventions. Maintenance, correction and renewal make reliability possible, yet often remain in the background of everyday life. The illusion lies in taking stability for granted and overlooking the conditions that sustain it. This relationship becomes particularly apparent under conditions of digitalisation. Algorithms influence which information becomes visible, while generative AI helps shape expressions and interpretations. Digital procedures can facilitate access while also creating new barriers. In this way, possibilities for action change even as the familiar surface of an order remains intact. This theoretical and conceptual article brings together sociological and philosophical approaches with selected empirical studies and thought examples. At its centre is the question of which order interventions sustain, whom it serves and who bears their consequences. The article develops criteria for responsible stabilisation: reliability must be accompanied by decisions that can be justified, effective opportunities to challenge them and a willingness to revise them. Choosing not to intervene can also be part of such an approach. Keywords: stability; social order; intervention; form; responsibility; sociotechnical systems; sociology; philosophy

AI has become a core component of consumer-facing marketing activities ranging from personalised product recommendations, conversational shopping assistants, targeted advertising, dynamic content and predictive offers. These uses of AI can affect how consumers search, consider and choose between different products. Yet, the extent to which these AI applications will affect purchase behaviour will not only depend on their technological capabilities. For AI-based marketing to influence consumer choice, consumers need to view the marketing communications as relevant, trustworthy and useful (see Ribeiro et al., 2025, for similar findings). The study investigates the effect of AI-enabled personalisation on purchase intention in consumers with specific focus on consumer trust and perceived value. The study will adopt a quantitative, cross-sectional approach. The population of the study is consumers who have encountered the use of AI-enabled recommendations or personalised marketing on digital channels. A structured questionnaire of five-point Likert scale will be used and a sample size of 250 respondents was used as an example for the statistical analysis alone because the primary data was not provided. Descriptive statistic, Pearson correlation and multiple regressions are proposed to be used.The results shown on this page, the following positive effects are observed between the variables: AI personalisation -> trust -> perceived value -> purchase intention. This is based on the example regression analysis results showing perceived value and trust have a great impact on purchase intention, AI personalisation has a positive direct relationship as well. However, bear in mind that these results are only an example, and should never be reported as actual research.

Many researchers have sought to integrate the interpretive depth of qualitative analysis with the analytical rigor of quantitative methods. We present The Interactive Thematic Analysis Network (TITAN), a novel software platform and methodological framework that extends completed thematic analyses through interactive network visualization and quantitative structural analysis. TITAN automatically transforms hierarchical qualitative coding outputs into multilevel node-and-edge networks, computes network metrics for excerpts, codes, themes, and higher-order groupings, and preserves direct traceability to the underlying qualitative evidence. The software was evaluated using a completed qualitative case study conducted for the U.S. Irregular Warfare Center (IWC), demonstrating automated transformation of thematic analysis outputs into an interactive network representation. We describe TITAN’s software architecture, analytical workflow, and analytical capabilities, showing how network science extends conventional thematic analysis by revealing structural relationships not readily identifiable using existing qualitative analysis software.

Reflexivity was built for a researcher whose instruments were of a different kind than her object. That assumption has quietly failed. When a researcher uses a large language model to code griefbots, recommender systems, or synthetic media, instrument and object come from the same technical population, and the properties her codebook detects (retention by default, smoothness, ambiguous reply status) are simultaneously operating inside the coding. I call this her infrastructural position, and it is not a variant of the social position reflexivity has long theorised. Participant objectivation ascends to a meta-level, an ascent available because the researcher is not a case in her own study. Infrastructural position denies the ascent; the move it permits is lateral. Against the regress objection, catalogued in the sociology of scientific knowledge three decades ago and unresolved there, I distinguish two ambitions. The completeness model seeks self-transparency and is destroyed by the regress. The calibration model is not, because it claims no epistemic privilege at all: it replaces transparency with auditability, and replaces a terminus with a published claim-to-level dependency map. This concedes Lynch’s case against reflexivity as a source of privileged knowledge and reconstructs a method on the far side of it. I demonstrate the model with tool-as-case: turning the algorithm audit on the auditor’s own instrument, under criteria published in object-facing form first. The sharpest consequence is not that model-assisted omission is uncheckable, true of human coding too, but that it is correlated across every study using the same model.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study was conducted to examine the effect of Game-Based Learning (GBL) on students’ intrinsic motivation, behavioral engagement, and emotional engagement, as well as the mediating role of intrinsic motivation in these relationships. The study was prompted by the phenomenon of learning loss following the COVID-19 pandemic, which has led to a decline in motivation and engagement among students at SMKN 2 Kota Kediri. A quantitative approach using SEM-PLS analysis was employed, with a questionnaire serving as the data collection instrument. The theoretical framework used is Self-Determination Theory (SDT) by Ryan & Deci. The study found that GBL has a significant positive effect on intrinsic motivation (f² = 1.328), behavioral engagement (f² = 0.382), and emotional engagement (f² = 0.109). Intrinsic motivation was found to have a significant effect on emotional engagement, but not on behavioral engagement. Mediation analysis indicated that intrinsic motivation partially mediates the effect of GBL on emotional engagement, whereas on the behavioral engagement pathway, intrinsic motivation was not found to act as a mediator. These findings imply that GBL is a learning method considered effective in enhancing learners’ motivation and engagement.

Driver behavior on public roadways requires closer attention to how self-monitoring, attentional control, and individual differences relate to unsafe driving outcomes. This study examined how metacognitive awareness, attentional lapses, mindfulness, temporal focus, and ADHD diagnosis relate to aggressive driving behavior. Participants completed questionnaires assessing metacognitive regulation, cognitive failures, mindfulness, temporal focus, and aggressive driving behavior. Findings indicated that attentional lapses were the strongest predictor of aggressive driving behavior. ADHD diagnosis was no longer a significant predictor after cognitive and self-regulatory variables were included in the model. These results suggest that aggressive driving behavior was more strongly linked to attentional lapses and monitoring failures than to ADHD diagnosis alone. Overall, the findings from this study suggest that aggressive driving behavior is meaningfully influenced by the combination of cognitive lapses, self-monitoring, and individual driver characteristics. Implications include improved driver assessment tools and attentional regulation training for drivers.

This article examines the role of tutors in fostering students’ intrinsic motivation to learn and improving academic performance in higher education institutions. It explains the nature of intrinsic motivation and the personal, pedagogical, and organizational factors that influence it. It also substantiates approaches through which tutors can work individually with students, support goal setting, provide feedback, and identify difficulties at an early stage. Trends in student enrolment in higher education are analysed in a table, and the importance of tutors’ individualised approach and academic support is discussed.

Based on the studies on the Production-Oriented Approach (POA) included in the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and combining bibliometrics with close reading, this paper examines the research characteristics, conceptual evolution, and digital-intelligent turn of this theory. The findings show that POA research has moved from rapid growth into a stage of stable deepening, with core authors and institutions becoming concentrated, and research themes expanding from college English to teaching Chinese to speakers of other languages, less commonly taught languages, textbook development, and intelligent teaching. Centered on the problem of 'separating learning from use,' the theory has refined its teaching principles, hypotheses, and procedures, forming a four-dimensional teaching framework that links learning, use, and assessment in a closed loop, together with a unit-nested teaching procedure. Generative artificial intelligence can empower teaching, yet existing studies are mostly short-cycle, single-course, and small-sample practices. Future research should carry out cross-language and cross-stage long-cycle comparisons, and build a human-machine collaborative assessment system based on classroom production, so as to address problems such as data bias, the weakening of teachers' subjectivity, and technology dependence.

Background: Emergency departments represent a critical point of access to healthcare in Canada, yet escalating pressures from overcrowding are putting patients at increased risk of preventable harm due to increased waiting times. Emergency department waiting rooms are evolving from passive holding spaces to extensions of the clinical care environment however, these spaces are not optimized to facilitate patient safety (Zamani, 2019), putting vulnerable individuals waiting for care at risk of deterioration and adverse outcomes. Waiting room safety netting emerges as a nascent, fragmented idea in the literature yet lacks the specificity and contextual grounding to be operationalized to quality improvement initiatives and patient safety planning. This study aimed to explicate the concept of an ED Waiting Room Safety Net utilizing Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis to identify the antecedents, attributes and consequences of this construct to inform a systems-oriented, contextually adaptable model for patient safety in emergency care. Methods: Rodger’s evolutionary concept analysis was chosen as the method focuses on concepts emerging through praxis rather than discrete conceptualization acknowledging that meaning arises through practice. Concept analysis occurs through six phases: identifying the concept and related terms, selecting the context and sample for data collection, gathering relevant data, analyzing for attributes, antecedents, and consequences, identifying an exemplar, and determining implications for future development. Results: 52 studies were identified through PubMed using combinations of surrogate terms, 18 scholarly works between 2017 and 2025, were selected and synthesized to derive the antecedents, attributes and consequences of a waiting room safety net. The Waiting Room Safety Net can be defined as: A proactive, responsive, and structured patient safety construct that involves optimizing human factors, technology, organizational processes, and the physical environment such that they interact to facilitate protective oversight of individuals in the emergency department waiting room and enable the avoidance of preventable harm while making the waiting experience more amenable to patients. The synthesis of 18 studies revealed eight thematic attributes which were consolidated into a conceptual model.
